questions.question_text:
A netballer took $16$ shots at goal during a match and scored $14$ of them.
Express her scoring shots as a percentage.

options.why: Found the percentage of shots missed ($2$ out of $16$) instead of those scored.
Divided $14$ by $16$ correctly but did not multiply by $100$.
Expressed the remaining $78$ as a percentage of $130$ instead of the $52$.

questions.question_text:
A cyclist rode $84$ km on Sunday and $56$ km on Saturday.
Express Sunday's distance as a percentage of Saturday's.

options.why: Wrote $\dfrac{56}{84}$, comparing Saturday with Sunday instead.
Formed $\dfrac{84}{56}$ correctly but did not multiply by $100$.

questions.question_text:
A soccer squad has $25$ players, and $22$ of them attended training.
What percentage of the squad did not attend?

options.why: Found the percentage who did attend instead of those who did not.
Gave the number who missed training ($3$) as a percentage without dividing by $25$.

questions.question_text:
A training run is $12$ km long.
An athlete has run $3000$ m of it.
Express the distance run as a percentage of the whole run.

options.why: This uses $1200$ m as the whole: $3000\div1200\times100=250\%$. But $12$ km is $12000$ m, so the correct percentage is $25\%$.
Inverted the fraction, comparing the whole run with the distance already run.

questions.question_text:
In a science experiment, $30$ g of Chemical A is mixed with $70$ g of Chemical B.
Jimmy calculates the percentage of Chemical A in the mixture as $42.86\%$.
Which statement explains his error?

options.text: He divided by the mass of Chemical B instead of the whole mixture of $100$ g.
He should divide by the mass of Chemical A instead of Chemical B.
options.why: Uses the part being compared as the denominator instead of the whole mixture.

options.text: He should use the mass of Chemical B as the numerator instead of Chemical A.
options.why: Changes the requested chemical from A to B instead of correcting the denominator.

questions.solution_text:
Jimmy used $\dfrac{30}{70}$, dividing by Chemical B only. The whole mixture is $30+70=100$ g.
He should use $\dfrac{30}{100}$ because the denominator must be the mass of the whole mixture.

questions.question_text:
A cup of flour is $360$ g.
Express one cup as a percentage of a $3$ kg bag of flour.

options.why: Calculated $360\div3\times100$ without converting kilograms to grams.
Divided $360$ by $3000$ but did not multiply by $100$.
Found the percentage of flour remaining after removing one cup instead of the percentage in one cup.
